headline: Building schools. Defending the right to teach.
summary: Black educators built schools, led classrooms and fought for pay, professional authority and jobs. These records follow named people and institutions—and show that opening schools to Black pupils did not automatically protect Black teachers.
coverageNote: Twelve documented episodes connect school founding, leadership, pay and desegregation to particular workplaces and decisions. Local victories and losses are distinguished from national rules; a reader’s own hiring history still needs evidence.
question: Which appointment records, board minutes, salary schedules or court-compliance reports connect this history to your school?

events.title: Charlotte Forten teaches newly freed people at Penn School
events.people: Charlotte Forten; Penn School founders Laura Towne and Ellen Murray; St. Helena Island families
events.decisionMaker: Towne and Murray organized Penn School with support from Philadelphia’s Port Royal Relief Committee.
events.barrier: Enslaved South Carolinians had been denied lawful access to literacy; freedom and schooling remained uncertain during the war.
events.change: Forten joined the school on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, as classes moved into Brick Baptist Church.
events.outcome: A Black educator taught freedpeople at a named workplace and recorded the experience in journals and her 1864 published account.
events.limit: Penn was a wartime school supported by a relief organization. This is not proof of employment by today’s Beaufort County school district.

source.title: National Park Service · Charlotte Forten Grimké
source.locator: Paragraphs on the fall 1862 arrival, Brick Baptist Church and “Life on the Sea Islands”
source.supports: Forten’s arrival, teaching location and firsthand accounts.

sources.title: National Park Service · Education during the Port Royal Experiment
sources.locator: Penn School paragraphs: Towne’s April 1862 arrival through Forten joining in the fall
sources.supports: The founders, relief-committee backing, literacy restrictions and move to Brick Baptist Church.

events.title: The Marion Nine turn community money into a school
events.people: The Marion Nine, including Alexander H. Curtis and Thomas Speed, and their community
events.decisionMaker: Nine formerly enslaved founders organized the school in Marion, Alabama.
events.barrier: After emancipation, Black Southerners had to build educational opportunities within a society that restricted them.
events.change: The founders raised $500 to buy land for Lincoln Normal School.
events.outcome: The school opened with 113 students and became the institution now known as Alabama State University.
events.limit: The opening documents an educational institution, not a teaching appointment for every student or a national first in Black education.

source.title: Alabama State University · History & Traditions
source.supports: The founders, fundraising, opening date and reported enrollment; the institution’s account of its predecessor.

events.title: State support for Black teacher education comes with a transfer of control
events.people: Peyton Finley, Lincoln’s trustees and the American Missionary Association
events.decisionMaker: Alabama’s State Board of Education passed the act accepting the Marion school.
events.barrier: Financial difficulty threatened the institution; Finley had pressed for state support for Black higher education.
events.change: The act provided a state normal school and university for Black teachers and students, conditional on transferring the buildings and grounds to state control.
events.outcome: A state-appointed, majority-white commission took charge and replaced the school’s president.
events.limit: Public funding expanded institutional support while reducing the founders’ control; it did not integrate Alabama’s white university.

source.title: Knight v. State of Alabama · historical findings
source.type: Court findings based on historical evidence
source.supports: Finley’s advocacy, the 1873 funding arrangement, transfer of property and change in governance.

events.title: Maria Baldwin moves from teacher to principal in Cambridge
events.decisionMaker: Cambridge’s School Committee urged Baldwin to accept the principalship of the Agassiz School.
events.barrier: Baldwin had struggled to obtain teaching work in Cambridge after completing teacher training.
events.change: Her 1889 appointment put a Black woman in charge of a public school attended mainly by white children.
events.outcome: She led the Agassiz School. In 2002 the committee renamed its later building the Maria L. Baldwin School.
events.limit: This documents a specific appointment and a school-name connection in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The present building is not the one where she began; it does not prove any current employee’s hiring route.

source.title: Cambridge Historical Commission · Maria Baldwin House evaluation
source.locator: February 25, 2022 report, pages 6–7; 1889 appointment and May 21, 2002 school renaming
source.supports: Training and employment obstacles, the principalship, and the Agassiz-to-Baldwin school connection across different buildings.

events.title: Anna Julia Cooper’s college-preparatory leadership meets a board’s opposition
events.people: Anna Julia Cooper, teacher and principal at M Street High School in Washington, D.C.
events.decisionMaker: Washington’s Board of Education dismissed Cooper as principal.
events.barrier: Cooper defended Black students’ access to college preparation amid pressure to prioritize vocational education.
events.change: Her dismissal removed a Black woman’s authority over the school’s educational direction.
events.outcome: She taught elsewhere and later returned to M Street as a teacher, continuing her educational work after losing the principalship.
events.limit: This records a contested leadership role, not uninterrupted advancement. The biography is not the board’s personnel file or proof of a present-day teacher’s appointment.

source.title: National Park Service · Dr. Anna Julia Cooper
source.locator: Early Life and Education, final paragraph; Women’s Clubs and Activism, final paragraph
source.type: Federal historical biography with scholarly references
source.supports: M Street teaching, the curriculum dispute, the 1906 dismissal and later return to teaching.

events.title: A community campaign creates a school and teaching posts in Atlanta
events.people: Atlanta’s Black voters and organizers; principal Charles L. Harper and his faculty
events.decisionMaker: Atlanta’s school board funded the school; Harper selected its teachers.
events.barrier: Black Atlantans had pressed for public secondary education while the city withheld a high school for them.
events.change: After voter organizing and a school-bond campaign, the board funded Booker T. Washington High School.
events.outcome: The school opened in 1924; its historical nomination records Harper’s recruitment of the faculty.
events.limit: This establishes a specific Atlanta workplace, not a connection to other schools with the same name or a list of every teacher hired.

source.title: Booker T. Washington High School · National Register nomination
source.supports: Community organizing, the opening of the Atlanta school and Harper’s recruitment of its faculty.

events.title: Melvin Alston and Norfolk teachers challenge a racial pay schedule
events.people: Melvin O. Alston, the Norfolk Teachers’ Association and lawyers including Thurgood Marshall and William H. Hastie
events.decisionMaker: The Fourth Circuit, in an opinion by Judge John J. Parker, reviewed the district court’s dismissal.
events.barrier: The teachers alleged that Norfolk paid Black teachers less despite equal qualifications, experience and duties.
events.change: The court held that a race-based salary policy would violate equal protection and that signing a teaching contract did not waive the right to challenge it.
events.outcome: The dismissal was reversed and the case returned for further proceedings.
events.limit: The opinion describes the legal route to relief; it is not a payroll record proving when every Norfolk teacher received equal pay.

source.title: Alston v. School Board of City of Norfolk, 112 F.2d 992
source.locator: Opinion, pages 993–997; concluding reversal and remand
source.supports: The teachers’ allegations, constitutional ruling and reversal; it does not document subsequent payroll compliance.

events.title: Atlanta changes its pay policy, but teachers still contest the result
events.people: Teachers William H. Reeves and Samuel Davis
events.decisionMaker: Atlanta’s Board of Education changed its salary system; federal courts later reviewed Davis’s challenge.
events.barrier: Separate salary schedules and disputed individual classifications left Black teachers challenging unequal pay.
events.change: After Reeves sued in 1942, the board abolished its separate schedules and directed a single salary plan.
events.outcome: Davis brought a further challenge in 1943; in 1949 the Fifth Circuit set aside a favorable decree pending exhaustion of administrative remedies.
events.limit: A new policy did not settle whether teachers actually received equal pay; this decision does not establish the eventual payroll outcome.

source.title: Cook v. Davis, 178 F.2d 595
source.supports: The 1942 policy change, Davis’s later challenge and the 1949 disposition; eventual equal pay is not established.

events.title: Brown changes pupils’ rights; teachers’ employment still needs its own evidence
events.people: Black children and families challenging segregated schools in Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia and Delaware
events.decisionMaker: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously, with Chief Justice Earl Warren writing the opinion.
events.barrier: State-enforced segregation excluded Black children from schools on racial grounds.
events.change: The Court held segregated public schooling unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment.
events.outcome: The decision rejected the legal basis for segregating pupils; the Court addressed implementation separately in 1955.
events.limit: Brown is not proof that every Black teacher kept a job, gained a promotion or received equal pay. Chambers and Singleton below address staffing harms during desegregation.

source.title: National Archives · Brown v. Board of Education
source.locator: May 17, 1954 opinion transcript: syllabus and opening paragraphs; introductory account of Brown II
source.type: Court opinion in federal archival custody
source.supports: The pupil-access holding and separate implementation proceedings; no teacher-employment outcome is established here.

events.title: Septima Clark loses her teaching job for refusing to leave the NAACP
events.people: Septima Poinsette Clark; Highlander Folk School director Myles Horton
events.decisionMaker: South Carolina enacted an affiliation ban for public employees; Clark’s teaching contract was not renewed when she refused to resign from the NAACP.
events.barrier: A public-school livelihood was made conditional on giving up civil-rights organizing.
events.change: After losing her job, Clark became Highlander’s full-time workshop director and later led citizenship education at SCLC.
events.outcome: She trained educators outside the public-school system. In 1976 South Carolina restored her teacher’s pension after recognizing her unjust termination.
events.limit: This was a loss followed by work elsewhere and a later remedy. It does not identify every affected teacher, establish a current district’s liability or replace Clark’s personnel records.

source.title: Stanford King Institute · Septima Poinsette Clark
source.locator: Paragraphs beginning “In 1956,” “By the time of her firing,” and “After retiring from SCLC”
source.type: Research-institute biography citing oral history and personal papers
source.supports: The nonrenewal, Highlander and SCLC employment, and 1976 pension restoration.

sources.title: South Carolina General Assembly · H. 4026 honoring Septima Clark
sources.locator: 2019 adopted resolution; clauses on the 1956 law, Highlander, SCLC and restored benefits
sources.supports: The legislature’s retrospective account; this is not the original dismissal order or a payroll record.

events.title: Hendersonville teachers challenge dismissal during desegregation
events.people: Black teacher plaintiffs, the North Carolina Teachers Association and attorney J. LeVonne Chambers
events.decisionMaker: The Fourth Circuit reversed the dismissal of their case against Hendersonville’s city school board.
events.barrier: After school integration, only 8 of 24 Black teachers were retained; all white teachers seeking reemployment kept their jobs.
events.change: The court required the same objective employment standards for Black and white teachers and rejected a racial staffing quota.
events.outcome: It directed reemployment for qualifying plaintiffs who wanted to return in 1966–67, assessment of damages and continuing court supervision.
events.limit: The ruling orders relief; it does not prove compliance. This was Hendersonville’s historical city system, not an established link to every school in today’s Henderson County district.

source.title: Chambers v. Hendersonville City Board of Education, 364 F.2d 189
source.locator: Majority opinion, paragraphs 6–12; counsel listed above the opinion
source.supports: Staffing losses, unequal selection standards and the ordered employment remedy; subsequent implementation remains unverified.

events.title: Singleton requires safeguards when desegregation cuts or changes jobs
events.people: Black educators affected by desegregation; student plaintiffs including Derek Jerome Singleton and their lawyers
events.decisionMaker: The Fifth Circuit directed staffing provisions in consolidated school-desegregation cases.
events.barrier: Staff reductions and demotions could remove Black educators while a district reorganized its schools.
events.change: The court required nondiscriminatory employment decisions and objective criteria for reductions, with evaluations retained for review.
events.outcome: The order protected qualified displaced staff when vacancies arose and treated lost responsibility or out-of-certification assignment as possible demotion—not just reduced pay.
events.limit: These are historical requirements, not proof of a particular educator’s reinstatement or a rule automatically applicable to every district today. Local orders and compliance records remain necessary.

source.title: Singleton v. Jackson Municipal Separate School District, 419 F.2d 1211
source.locator: Opinion dated December 1, 1969 in the text; Part I, “Desegregation of Faculty and Other Staff,” paragraphs 2–3
source.supports: The historical staffing safeguards and demotion definition; the site’s February 1970 header differs from the opinion date.

furtherResearch: Read Penn School registers and Forten’s original writings to connect named students, teachers and teaching locations.
Check appointment and board records for Baldwin and Cooper; distinguish school continuity, renaming and replacement buildings from an individual’s employment history.
Find Norfolk and Atlanta payrolls and subsequent proceedings to establish when salary policies changed actual pay.
Read Hendersonville and other districts’ compliance reports, staffing lists and personnel files for reinstatement, displacement and promotion after court orders.
Establish your school’s exact city, district, former names and any merger before attaching a historical workplace connection.
